content: 1. The combination of improved sanitation and the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater significantly reduces the burden of diseases associated with poor hygiene and sanitation. 2. Enhanced nutrition and food security play a critical role in reducing children's susceptibility to various diseases. 3. Between 1990 and 2015, efforts to reduce maternal mortality rates by three-fourths were supported by improved health and nutrition linked to waste-fed agriculture and aquaculture, which help mitigate conditions like anemia and other health issues affecting maternal mortality. 4. Better nutrition and food security also reduce the risk of diseases that can complicate pregnancy. 5. The safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater, along with basic sanitation, helps prevent water-related diseases such as diarrheal diseases, schistosomiasis, filariasis, trachoma, intestinal worm infections, and foodborne trematode infections. 6. Improved health and nutrition reduce the severity and susceptibility to HIV/AIDS and other major diseases. 7. Increased awareness and knowledge of better water management practices support community-based environmental management approaches to reduce malaria transmission risks. 8. The safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater alleviates pressure on freshwater resources and reduces health risks for downstream communities. 9. Improved sanitation, particularly in the context of safe excreta use, reduces the flow of human waste into waterways, thereby protecting both human and environmental health. 10. Effective water management, including pollution control and water conservation, is essential for maintaining ecosystem integrity. 11. Waste-fed peri-urban agriculture can significantly improve the livelihoods of slum dwellers. 12. Development agendas and partnerships must recognize the fundamental role of safe wastewater, excreta, and greywater use in agriculture and aquaculture, as well as basic sanitation, in driving economic and social development. 13. Stimulating opportunities for the safe use of waste in agricultural production enhances options for self-employment. 14. Adherence to WHO Guidelines facilitates international trade in agricultural produce derived from waste-fed systems. 15. Schistosomiasis is a chronic tropical disease affecting the liver, lungs, urinary system, or central nervous system, caused by parasitic flatworms. 16. Filariasis is a disease caused by thread-like worms transmitted by mosquitoes, leading to chronic swelling of the lower extremities due to lymphatic vessel invasion. 17. Trachoma is a contagious bacterial infection of the cornea and conjunctiva, causing granulation and scarring. 18. Implementing WHO Guidelines maximizes the health and environmental benefits of using wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture by preventing disease transmission and exposure to hazardous chemicals. 19. The use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture is widespread, both formally and informally, and contributes to nutrient and water recycling, improving household nutrition and food security. 20. International policies on waste-fed agriculture must address the safe trade of food products while considering potential negative health impacts. 21. Cost-effective interventions are available to control the negative health impacts associated with wastewater, excreta, and greywater use. 22. National consumer protection legislation has international implications for policies governing the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater. 23. The WHO Guidelines aim to establish national standards and regulations that are protective of public health and can be readily implemented and enforced. 24. Successful implementation of the Guidelines requires a broad-based policy framework with incentives and sanctions to alter behavior, monitor progress, and improve situations. 25. Intersectoral coordination and cooperation at national and local levels, along with the development of suitable skills and expertise, are essential for implementing the Guidelines. 26. The regulatory framework should adopt a safe reuse of wastewater plan format, aligned with water safety plans in other areas of water quality management and health protection. 27. In many cases, full implementation of the Guidelines may not be immediately feasible, requiring progressive, systematic, and incremental approaches based on current realities and available resources. 28. The greatest health threats should be prioritized and addressed first, with cost-effective measures substituted over time as risk assessment and management processes evolve. 29. Standards for regulating wastewater, excreta, and greywater use have evolved into management strategies, supported by the development of new technologies. 30. Policies for the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture must be flexible and responsive to new situations and developments. 31. More than 10% of the global population consumes food produced using wastewater irrigation, with higher percentages in low-income countries with arid climates. 32. Population growth will drive increased demand for water resources, necessitating better integration of wastewater management into overall water resource management. 33. Traditional use of excreta in agriculture and aquaculture has been practiced for centuries and continues in many countries, particularly in urban and peri-urban areas. 34. Adequately treating sludge from on-site sanitation systems to produce safe biosolids or compost is crucial for improving public health. 35. On-site sanitation systems, such as double-pit latrines, require less water and are increasingly seen as alternatives to waterborne sewerage, especially in arid regions. 36. Waste-fed aquaculture is declining due to urbanization and the shift to high-input aquaculture, but unintentional use of polluted surface waters in aquaculture is increasing. 37. Policy formulation for wastewater, excreta, and greywater use requires sound analysis of local trends and viable risk management solutions. 38. Wastewater, excreta, and greywater are reliable year-round water sources containing nutrients essential for plant and fish growth, supporting food production in urban and peri-urban areas. 39. Irrigation with wastewater can supply all the nutrients required for crop growth, reducing the need for additional fertilizers. 40. The use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture reduces downstream environmental and health impacts while supporting food security. 41. Policies promoting the beneficial application of wastewater, excreta, and greywater should link environmental and health protection with food security and consumer protection to maximize health benefits and reduce infectious disease risks.
